implementation_notes: The Scala form is common around case classes, because the fields are public vals by construction and any method can read any of them. The move is an inherent method on the case class or a function in its companion, which is where Scala already puts constructors, equality and pattern-matching helpers — so the behaviour ends up in a place Scala programmers look first. When the rule must be swappable, a typeclass parameter is the honest encoding of 'the behaviour is deliberately outside the type'.
idiom_name: method on A reading B’s case-class fields
code_sketch:
case class Report(title: String)
case class Date(y: Int, m: Int, d: Int)

def label(r: Report, dt: Date): String = s"${r.title} ${dt.y}-${dt.m}"  // envious

object Date { def iso(dt: Date): String = /* companion holds the rule */ }
pitfalls: Case-class `copy()` lets any caller construct an inconsistent value, which is why the destination for a moved invariant is often a smart constructor in the companion rather than a method.
Extension methods in Scala 3 make the envy invisible to readers; prefer companion-object methods on your own types.
Pattern-matching exhaustivity is a compiler feature the rule gives up when the rule moves onto another type — check that the moved rule keeps its matches exhaustive.
